fixes.explanation: Right, they did not remember. The psalm says, "Our fathers in Egypt did not grasp Your wonders or remember Your abundant kindness; but they rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea." They saw wonders up close and still didn't grasp them. I've hopped into a room and forgotten why, but this is a whole other level.
Yes. The psalm says they "…rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea." That's right at the water, and the writer admits it plainly. I think that honesty is what makes the rescue after it so big.
The psalm doesn't put it at the Jordan. It says they "…rebelled by the sea, there at the Red Sea." The spot is the Red Sea, friend.

I get why you'd think it, after that rebellion. But the verse says, "Yet He saved them for the sake of His name, to make His power known." The reason it gives is His name and His power. The word is power.

Right, not one. The psalm says, "The waters covered their foes; not one of them remained." God saved Israel from the hand that hated them, and none of those foes remained. It's a heavy scene, so I'll just say it plainly.
Yes, tested. The psalm says they "…craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert." Craving and testing, both in one verse. I think that's a hard one to sit with, friend.
Wouldn't that be nice? But the psalm says they "…craved intensely in the wilderness and tested God in the desert." Verse 12 had them singing His praise. By verse 14 they're testing Him.

Right. The psalm says, "In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD." Moses was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), and Aaron is called the holy one of the LORD. Those are the two the camp envied.

Those two aren't the ones the psalm names. It says, "In the camp they envied Moses, as well as Aaron, the holy one of the LORD." Moses was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), and Aaron is called the holy one of the LORD. That's who the people envied.

Right, he doesn't get away. The psalm says, "The earth opened up and swallowed Dathan; it covered the assembly of Abiram." The earth swallowed him, so Dathan did not escape. I think this one is meant to make us pause, friend.
Yes. The psalm says, "At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image." They made it, and then they worshiped it. That's a lot of trust to put in something they had just made.
Nice try, friend, but no lampstand in this verse. The psalm says, "At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image." The image was a calf, plain and simple.
Yes, forgot. The psalm says, "They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt…" They forgot the very One who did those great things. It's the same trouble we saw back at the sea.

Yes. The psalm says, "So He said He would destroy them—had not Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them." Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), stood in the gap. I think that's a whole lot of courage.

That's not who the psalm names. It says Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath. Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is the one who stood in the gap.

Not Elijah, friend. The psalm says Moses His chosen one stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them. Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is the one who stood in the gap. That's the answer.
Right. The psalm says, "They despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His promise." They despised the land and did not believe what God promised. That's the whole problem in one verse.
True. The psalm says, "But Phinehas stood and intervened, and the plague was restrained." I like how plain it is. He stood, he stepped in, and the psalm says the plague was restrained.
The psalm says the opposite. "But Phinehas stood and intervened, and the plague was restrained." He stepped in, and the plague was restrained. So the answer is true.
Yes. The psalm says, "It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come." That's a long stretch of credit. I'd settle for a few weeks of good reviews on my cookies.

No, friend. The psalm says, "It was credited to him as righteousness for endless generations to come." His stand was counted as righteousness, not weakness. And that credit lasts for endless generations.

Yes. The psalm says, "For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips." Even Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), had a moment with his words. Every one of us has said something and wished it back, friend, and I think I've said it to a mixing bowl.

That's not in this verse. The psalm says, "For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips." At Meribah, Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), spoke rashly.

Not in this verse. The psalm says, "For they rebelled against His Spirit, and Moses spoke rashly with his lips." Moses, who was sent to lead Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), spoke rashly at the waters of Meribah.

Yes. The psalm says, "…but they mingled with the nations and adopted their customs." They blended in with the very peoples the LORD had commanded them to destroy. It's like adding too many ingredients until you can't find the recipe anymore.
The LORD had commanded them to destroy the peoples, and the psalm says they did not. It says, "…but they mingled with the nations and adopted their customs." They mingled instead.
No, a shield protects. But the psalm says the idols "…became a snare to them." A snare is a trap, not a shield.
Not here. The psalm says, "They worshiped their idols, which became a snare to them." Instead of a blessing, the idols were a trap. A snare is a trap, and that's what the psalm says they became.

Right, His anger did burn. The psalm says, "So the anger of the LORD burned against His people, and He abhorred His own inheritance." The psalm doesn't pretend that sin is small. I think it's why the mercy that comes later hits so hard.

No new law in this verse, friend. The psalm says, "Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress." He didn't answer with a rulebook. The psalm says He heard them and took note of their distress.

Offerings are a fair guess, but the psalm points somewhere else. It says, "And He remembered His covenant with them, and relented by the abundance of His loving devotion." Their offerings never come up in the verse. What He remembers is His covenant, and I think that's a relief to read.
The psalm says the opposite. "He made them objects of compassion to all who held them captive." That covers all who held them captive. So the answer is true.

Yes, thanks is the reason. The psalm says, "Save us, O LORD our God, and gather us from the nations, that we may give thanks to Your holy name, that we may glory in Your praise." The prayer ends up back at thanks, right where the psalm began (Psalm 106:1). That's a nice loop to notice.
